subject: MGMT464
title: Hurdle 4 · The Fork in the Pass — Contingency Leadership Theories

questions.stem: Identify the three variables every contingency model matches.
options: The leader, the followers and the situation
The task, the time available and the money available
The leader's traits, roles and skills
Power, politics and networks in the organisation
questions.why: Three variables, every model. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Describe what contingency leadership theories attempt to explain.
options: The appropriate leadership style based on the leader, followers and situation
The one best style that works for every leader in every situation with every follower
Which traits make leaders emerge from a group and which traits make them effective
How followers are born with the tendency to accept or resist direction
questions.why: It depends. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Identify what the 'situation' variable includes.
options: Task structure, the leader's position power, the organisation's climate, time pressure, decision quality required
Only the weather and physical conditions in which the work is done
Only the budget available to the leader for rewards and resources
Only the leader's personality and the way it interacts with the personalities of the followers in the team on the day
questions.why: What is happening around them. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Identify the question the Normative model asks.
options: How much participation should followers have in this decision?
Is the leader task-oriented or relationship-oriented by nature?
What does the follower need from the leader to reach the goal?
How much control should the boss give to followers over their own work?
questions.why: Vroom. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Describe the LPC scale.
options: Describing your least preferred co-worker kindly means relationship-oriented (high LPC); harshly means task-oriented (low LPC)
A measure of follower skill and readiness that tells the leader how much direction to give
A list of seven decision styles from boss-centred to subordinate-centred leadership
A grid of two concerns — for production and for people — with five named positions
questions.why: Fiedler treats the result as a stable trait. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Identify Fiedler's three situational favourableness variables.
options: Leader–member relations, task structure, position power
Expectancy, instrumentality and valence
Decision significance, importance of commitment and leader expertise
The leader's traits, behaviour and situation
questions.why: Eight combinations. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Identify the best style for moderately favourable situations in Fiedler's model.
options: Relationship-oriented
Task-oriented
Delegating
Laissez-faire or delegating
questions.why: Moderate (4–7) → relationship-oriented. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Explain Fiedler's controversial claim.
options: Leadership style is fixed, so change the situation — restructure the task, increase position power, or move the leader
Leaders can adopt any style, so training should teach every manager all of them
Followers choose the style, so the leader should ask them which they prefer
Situations never change, so the leader must be chosen to match them permanently
questions.why: Do not retrain the leader. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Describe the Leadership Continuum.
options: Seven points from boss-centred to subordinate-centred leadership; the leader can move along the line
Five grid styles from impoverished to team leader, with the team leader as the ideal that every manager should aim for
Two fixed styles — task-oriented and relationship-oriented — that the leader cannot change
Four path–goal styles chosen to fit the followers and the task
questions.why: Tannenbaum and Schmidt. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Identify point 5 on the continuum.
options: The leader presents the problem, gets suggestions, then decides
The leader makes the decision and announces it to the group
The leader permits the group to decide within limits the leader has defined
The leader sells the decision to the group after making it
questions.why: Point 5. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Identify the forces that decide the point on the line.
options: Forces in the leader, the followers and the situation
Only the leader's mood and confidence on the day of the decision
Only company policy on how decisions are made
Only the time pressure on the decision
questions.why: Later versions added the environment. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Describe the chapter's practical finding about managers on the continuum.
options: Most managers overestimate how far along the line they are — followers place them one or two points more boss-centred
Managers underestimate their own authority and sit further toward the subordinate end of the line than they think they do
Followers never notice where the manager sits on the line because they see only the decision
Everyone agrees on the point, because the leader's behaviour is visible to all and is discussed openly in the team
questions.why: In practice. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Identify the four Path–Goal styles.
options: Directive, supportive, participative, achievement-oriented
Decide, consult, facilitate, delegate
Autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire and servant leadership
Task-oriented, people-oriented, both, neither
questions.why: House. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Describe when the supportive style is used.
options: When the task is stressful, boring or unpleasant and followers need encouragement
When the task is unstructured and the followers are inexperienced and want clear direction from the leader
When followers are skilled and want involvement in decisions about the work
When followers are capable and motivated and the task is complex
questions.why: Encourages and cares. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Identify the theory Path–Goal builds on.
options: Expectancy theory — the leader clears the path from effort to reward
Equity theory — the leader makes sure every follower's path is as fair as the others'
Maslow's hierarchy — the leader clears the path from lower needs to higher ones
Reinforcement theory — the leader rewards every step along the path
questions.why: Builds directly on Chapter 3. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Describe how locus of control affects the Path–Goal choice.
options: Internal locus → participative; external locus → directive
Internal locus → directive; external locus → participative
Locus of control has no effect on the choice of style
Locus of control decides pay rather than style
questions.why: Subordinate situational factors. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Identify the five Normative model styles.
options: Decide, consult individually, consult group, facilitate, delegate
Directive, supportive, participative, achievement-oriented, coaching
Task, relationship, both, neither, mixed
Announce, sell, test, consult, join
questions.why: Vroom. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Describe the facilitate style.
options: The leader acts as facilitator; the group decides within the leader's boundaries
The leader decides alone and announces the decision to the group
The leader asks members one by one for their views, then decides
The group decides without any boundaries and the leader only provides the resources it asks for
questions.why: Who finally decides? The group. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Differentiate time-driven from development-driven decisions.
options: Time-driven: the fastest style the situation allows; development-driven: move toward facilitate or delegate even if slower
Time-driven always means delegate, because delegation saves the leader's time
Development-driven always means decide, because the leader develops by deciding
They are the same, because every decision has both a time and a development cost
questions.why: Time-driven vs development-driven. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Identify what a high 'importance of commitment' pushes toward.
options: Consult, facilitate or delegate
Decide alone and announce
Announce the decision and sell it
Ignore the group's preferences
questions.why: The seven questions. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Identify the two prescriptive models.
options: Fiedler's contingency model and Vroom's normative model
The Leadership Continuum and House's Path–Goal theory
The Ohio State and Michigan studies
The Leadership Grid and the Iowa studies of the three styles
questions.why: Prescriptive: a decision tree or matrix. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Describe the weakness of descriptive models.
options: Two managers can read the same situation differently
They are too rigid to fit real situations
They give exact answers that leave no room for judgement
They ignore the leader and look only at the followers
questions.why: Flexible, realistic — but subjective. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Describe substitutes for leadership.
options: Characteristics of the task, followers or organisation that replace the need for a leader — skilled followers, structured work, strong norms, cohesive teams
Leaders who replace other leaders when they leave the organisation or move to a new role
Rules and procedures that cancel the leader's influence even when it is needed
Deputies and assistants who act for the leader when the leader is absent
questions.why: Where they exist, directive or supportive behaviour adds little. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Identify examples of neutralisers of leadership.
options: Physical distance, rigid rules, followers indifferent to the leader's rewards, weak position power
Skilled followers and clear feedback from the task itself
Cohesive teams with strong norms of their own
Strong professional norms that guide the followers' work
questions.why: Neutralisers cancel influence even when needed. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Identify the Grid, Fiedler and Path–Goal names for the task-oriented column.
options: 9,1 authority-compliance; low-LPC task-oriented; directive or achievement-oriented
1,9 country club; high-LPC relationship-oriented; supportive, participative and warm
9,9 team leader; both orientations; participative
1,1 impoverished; neither orientation; delegate
questions.why: One map of the styles. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Identify the four-step method for an unseen case.
options: Describe leader, followers and situation with evidence; choose the model that fits the decision; apply it and name the style; justify
Guess the style from experience; defend it with the textbook; ignore the case details; conclude
List the leader's traits; rank them by importance; pick the top trait; justify the style it implies
Vote on the style with the group; decide; announce; move on to the next case
questions.why: Variables → model → style → justification. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Describe when to use Fiedler rather than Vroom or Path–Goal, according to the method.
options: Use Fiedler when the leader's style is fixed; Vroom when the question is how much to involve; Path–Goal for follower needs
Always Fiedler, because it is the only model that treats style as a trait
Always Vroom, because every leadership question is about participation
Never Path–Goal, because it duplicates what expectancy theory already says
questions.why: Choose the model that fits the decision. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Identify the best style for the least favourable situation (poor relations, unstructured task, weak power).
options: Task-oriented
Relationship-oriented
Participative
Delegating
questions.why: Situation 8 → task-oriented. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Describe when the achievement-oriented style is used.
options: When followers are capable and motivated and the task is complex
When followers are nervous, new and unsure of the system
When the task is boring, stressful or unpleasant
When the group is hostile to the leader and resists every direction it is given
questions.why: Sets challenging goals, shows confidence. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Explain what a leader should do when facing neutralisers.
options: Change the situation or find other sources of influence
Give up, because neutralisers cannot be overcome
Shout louder so that the followers pay attention
Add more rules and procedures so that the followers have no choice but to comply
questions.why: Fiedler again, or Chapter 5. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's reading of the cola case in question 1.
options: Both readings are contingency readings — the situation changed and the question is whether the leader's style fitted the new situation
The leader was simply bad and would have failed in any situation
Cola never changes, so the leader's style was the only variable
Traits decide everything, so the leader's success depended on who he was
questions.why: Answer to question 1. See §4.1.

questions.stem: Identify point 1 on the Leadership Continuum.
options: The leader makes the decision and announces it
The leader presents a tentative decision
The leader defines limits and asks the group to decide
The leader permits maximum freedom
questions.why: Boss-centred end. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Exercise 1A: a gas leak alarm sounds in a factory; the shift supervisor has trained for this and the team has not. Select the Normative style and the question that drove it.
options: Decide — time-driven; leader expertise high, commitment not needed
Delegate — the team learns best by doing, even in an emergency
Consult group — commitment matters when lives are at risk and the team must act together
Facilitate — development-driven, so the team should decide
questions.why: Answer key: A decide. See §4.5 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1B: a hospital department must redesign its booking process; nurses know the problems, resent the last top-down change, and the manager has no IT expertise. Select the Normative style.
options: Consult group or facilitate — commitment essential, leader lacks expertise, the group has it; development-driven
Decide — the manager is in charge and the redesign is her responsibility
Consult individually — it is faster than a group meeting and keeps control of the redesign firmly with the manager
Delegate with no boundaries, because the nurses know the problems best
questions.why: Answer key: B consult group or facilitate. See §4.5 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1C: eight senior engineers must choose a technical framework; the manager is ten years out of date; the deadline is comfortable. Select the Normative style.
options: Facilitate or delegate — group expertise and competence high, time available
Decide — managers decide, and the engineers will accept the framework
Consult individually — keep control of the decision while hearing each engineer's view in private
Announce and sell the framework the manager knows best
questions.why: Answer key: C facilitate or delegate. See §4.5 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1D: a nervous new call-centre recruit, unsure of the system, asks how to handle a complaint she has never seen. Select the Path–Goal style and the factor.
options: Directive — inexperienced follower who wants direction; the task is unstructured for her
Supportive — she is stressed by the complaint and needs encouragement before anything else is said
Participative — ask her ideas so that she learns to think for herself
Achievement-oriented — set a tough target so that she rises to it
questions.why: Answer key: D directive. See §4.4 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 1E: experienced sales agents are demoralised after a quarter of missed targets caused by a supply failure they could not control. Select the Path–Goal style.
options: Supportive — stressful situation, external cause, followers need encouragement
Directive — tell them exactly how to sell in the coming quarter, step by step
Achievement-oriented — raise the target sharply to restore their confidence in themselves
Participative — redesign the product and the sales approach with them
questions.why: Answer key: E supportive. See §4.4 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Determine which Exercise 1 case contains a substitute for leadership and what the leader should do with the freed time.
options: Case C — senior experts; the leader should focus on resources, boundaries and the next product
Case A — the gas alarm, which tells the team exactly what to do without any need for the leader's instructions
Case D — the recruit, who can follow the system without the leader
Case E — the supply failure, which explains the results without the leader
questions.why: Answer key, task 3. See §4.6 and Exercise 1.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: Dr Mariam is the new head of the Kalba clinic; the previous head decided everything alone and left; staff are wary; she can hire and reward; her LPC is high. Determine the three variables.
options: Leader: relationship-oriented (high LPC); followers: mixed — senior and junior doctors, nurses, receptionists, wary; situation: strong position power, untested relations, three different tasks
Leader: task-oriented (low LPC); followers: all experts who need no direction; situation: no position power and no deadlines
Leader: unknown style; followers: hostile to any new head; situation: easy, because the clinic runs itself
Leader: autocratic like the previous head; followers: loyal to the clinic; situation: stable and well structured
questions.why: Step 1: three variables with evidence. See §4.7 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2: Rate the clinic's situational favourableness for Fiedler and determine whether Dr Mariam's style fits.
options: Relations untested/poor, tasks mixed, power strong → moderate favourableness → a relationship-oriented leader fits reasonably
Most favourable → a task-oriented leader is needed, so she does not fit the clinic
Least favourable → she must be replaced by a task-oriented head
Favourableness cannot be rated until she has been in post for a year
questions.why: Marking guide, task 2. See §4.2 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Determine what Fiedler would change at the clinic if style and situation did not match.
options: Build relations or structure the tasks rather than change Dr Mariam
Send Dr Mariam on a course to change her style to task-oriented
Lower her position power so that the situation becomes less favourable
Hire a second head with a task-oriented style to share the job
questions.why: Change the situation, not the leader. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2, task (a): the electronic records system must be live in six weeks with training for everyone. Select the style and the deciding variable.
options: Directive / decide or consult individually — a hard deadline and low follower expertise
Facilitate — commitment to the new system is what matters most
Delegate — the nurses know the records best and should design the training programme themselves
Supportive — the change is stressful and staff need encouragement
questions.why: Marking guide: (a) directive/decide or consult individually. See §4.5 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2, task (b): patient waiting times have doubled and nobody agrees why. Select the style and why.
options: Participative / consult group or facilitate — commitment needed and the staff hold the knowledge
Decide — she has the authority and the waiting times cannot wait
Directive — tell the staff to work faster until the times fall
Delegate — walk away and let the staff fix it themselves
questions.why: Marking guide: (b) participative/consult group or facilitate. See §4.5 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Exercise 2, task (c): the two junior doctors need supervision on clinical protocols, while the senior doctors do not. Select the styles.
options: Juniors: directive with achievement-oriented coaching; seniors: delegate
Everyone: participative, so that juniors and seniors learn from each other
Everyone: supportive, because clinical work is stressful for all
Juniors: delegate so they learn; seniors: directive so standards are kept
questions.why: Marking guide: (c) directive with achievement coaching; seniors delegate. See §4.4 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Determine what would go wrong if Dr Mariam used her natural relationship-oriented style on all three tasks.
options: She would miss the records deadline and leave the juniors unsupervised
Nothing — relationships fix everything in a clinic of this size
The senior doctors would resign because they dislike being managed in such a warm, personal way
Waiting times would fall because staff would feel supported
questions.why: Marking guide, task 4. See §4.7 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Determine the substitute for leadership and the neutraliser in the Kalba clinic.
options: Substitute: the senior doctors' expertise; neutraliser: the wariness left by the previous head's autocracy, removed by early consultation
Substitute: the software vendor; neutraliser: the receptionists who resist the new system
Substitute: the six-week deadline; neutraliser: the budget for training
Substitute: Dr Mariam's high LPC; neutraliser: the training programme
questions.why: Marking guide, task 4. See §4.6 and Exercise 2.

questions.stem: Take-away: a project team's coordinator believes she operates at point 6 (team decides within limits); members say she really announces decisions. Determine the chapter's explanation.
options: Managers overestimate how far along the continuum they are; followers place them one or two points more boss-centred
Members are wrong, because the coordinator knows her own behaviour best
Point 6 does not exist in the version of the continuum the chapter uses
Teams cannot judge where a leader sits, because they see only the decisions
questions.why: In practice. See §4.3 and the take-away.

questions.stem: Take-away: the Project 2 interview with a real leader is unstructured and stressful; one member is confident, another is anxious. Determine the Path–Goal style for each.
options: Participative or achievement-oriented for the confident member; supportive (with some direction) for the anxious one
Directive for both, because an interview with a real leader needs a clear plan
Supportive for both, because interviews are stressful for everyone
Delegate for both, because students should manage their own project
questions.why: Which style — and for which member does it change. See §4.4 and the take-away.

questions.stem: Rami's three followers trust him, the climb is a familiar routine, and he can assign the food and the ropes. Rate the situation for Fiedler and select the best style.
options: Most favourable — good relations, structured task, strong power → task-oriented
Moderate favourableness → relationship-oriented
Least favourable → task-oriented
Cannot be rated without an LPC score for Rami
questions.why: Situations 1–3 → task-oriented. See §4.2.

questions.stem: At the fork in the pass, both paths look possible, the team must stay committed to whichever is chosen, and Noor knows these mountains better than Rami. Select the Normative style.
options: Consult group or facilitate — commitment matters and the group holds the expertise
Decide — the captain decides alone and the team follows whichever path he chooses without discussion
Delegate with no limits, because Noor knows the mountains best
Announce the path and sell it to the team on the way
questions.why: Commitment plus group expertise → consult or facilitate. See §4.5.

questions.stem: The rescue party reaches a village whose own guards are trained, drilled and organised; Rami's orders add nothing. Classify what the village guards represent.
options: A substitute for leadership — the leader's value moves to boundary work
A neutraliser that cancels Rami's influence over the guards of the village
A Path–Goal factor that calls for the directive style
An LPC score showing that the guards are task-oriented
questions.why: Where substitutes exist, directive behaviour adds little. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Rami sends orders by messenger to a team two days away who no longer care about his praise. Classify the problem.
options: Neutralisers — physical distance and indifference to the leader's rewards cancel his influence
A substitute — the team is skilled enough to manage without him
High favourableness — the team knows what to do
A descriptive model that the team is reading differently from Rami
questions.why: Neutralisers. See §4.6.

questions.stem: Omar is capable, motivated and faces the hardest climb of the journey. Select the Path–Goal style Rami should use.
options: Achievement-oriented — set a challenging goal and show confidence
Directive — tell him each handhold on the way up the hardest face
Supportive — comfort him before the climb
Participative — vote with the team on the route
questions.why: Capable, motivated, complex task → achievement-oriented. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Select the model to use when the decision is 'how much should the followers be involved in choosing the camp site?'.
options: The Normative model (Vroom)
Fiedler's contingency model
The Leadership Grid
Trait theory
questions.why: Choose the model that fits the decision. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Rami says 'we camp here — any questions?' with the decision already made. Determine the point on the Leadership Continuum.
options: Point 3 — presents ideas and invites questions; decision basically made
Point 7 — the group decides freely within the limits of the mission and the leader joins as a member
Point 5 — gets suggestions from the group, then decides
Point 1 — announces the decision with no questions allowed
questions.why: Point 3. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Rami has ten seconds before the rockfall; he knows the escape route; the team will follow whatever he says. Determine the Normative style and whether it is time- or development-driven.
options: Decide — time-driven
Facilitate — development-driven
Consult group — development-driven
Delegate — time-driven
questions.why: Fastest style the situation allows. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Identify the Normative model's names for the 'both' and 'relationship' columns of the style map.
options: Consult individually or consult group (both); facilitate (relationship); delegate (hands-off)
Decide (both); delegate (relationship); consult (hands-off)
Facilitate (both); decide (relationship); consult (hands-off)
Delegate (both); decide (relationship); facilitate (hands-off)
questions.why: One map of the styles. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Determine the model to use when the question is 'what does this frightened new follower need from me?'.
options: Path–Goal
Fiedler's contingency model
The Normative model
The Leadership Grid
questions.why: Follower needs → Path–Goal. See §4.7.

questions.stem: Rami's LPC score is high — he describes even the Crow chief kindly. Determine Fiedler's reading of his style.
options: Relationship-oriented
Task-oriented and directive
Participative
Delegating
questions.why: Describe them kindly → high LPC. See §4.2.

questions.stem: Rami says 'here are the limits — no fires, back by dusk — now you decide the route'. Determine the continuum point.
options: Point 6 — the leader defines the limits and asks the group to decide
Point 1 — the leader decides and announces
Point 3 — the leader presents ideas and invites questions
Point 7 — the group decides freely within the limits of the organisation
questions.why: Point 6. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Rami presents a tentative plan and says he is willing to change it. Determine the continuum point.
options: Point 4
Point 2
Point 6
Point 7
questions.why: Presents a tentative decision subject to change. See §4.3.

questions.stem: Dana must wade the cold river for the third time tonight; she is capable but miserable. Select the Path–Goal style.
options: Supportive — the task is unpleasant and she needs encouragement
Directive — she needs instructions on how to wade safely
Achievement-oriented — raise the target to a fourth crossing before dawn
Participative — ask for her ideas on how to cross
questions.why: Stressful, boring or unpleasant task. See §4.4.

questions.stem: Rami must choose which village to warn first; he has the knowledge, the team will accept any answer, and there is no time. Select the Normative style.
options: Decide
Facilitate
Delegate
Consult group
questions.why: Leader expertise high, commitment likely, time short. See §4.5.

questions.stem: Analyse a team so skilled that Rami's instructions only slow it down. Determine the correct response, according to the chapter.
options: Recognise the substitute and move the leader's value to boundary work — it is a contingency skill, not failure
Give more instructions so that the team remembers who is in charge
Replace the team with one that needs the leader's instructions
Abandon leadership entirely, because the team no longer needs a leader
questions.why: Recognising a substitute. See §4.6.
